title: Engineering non-Markovianity from spectral shaping of bosonic and fermionic baths
authors: Si Luo, Cun Long, Daochi Zhang, Massimiliano Di Ventra, Xiao Zheng
abstract: Non-Markovianity is the property that a physical system's future state depends on its previous dynamical history, namely the system has memory of its past. It is a key resource for quantum technologies but it is difficult to engineer without specific strategies. Here, we show that introducing a band gap in the environmental spectral density of both bosonic and fermionic baths provides a direct route to tuning non-Markovianity over a wide range. We demonstrate this effect by means of numerical simulations across bosonic and fermionic environments and discuss experimental tests of our predictions.
summary: This paper demonstrates that non-Markovianity, a key resource in quantum physics, can be engineered by modifying the spectral density of the environment bath. By introducing a controlled band gap via spectral shaping, the authors show they can tune the memory effects in both bosonic and fermionic systems. This technique offers a powerful theoretical tool for designing quantum devices with specific memory characteristics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of engineering non-Markovianity—the memory effect in a system's evolution—which is crucial for quantum technologies but difficult to control.
main_result: Introducing a band gap by spectrally shaping the bath environment (both bosonic and fermionic) provides a direct, tunable route to achieving strong non-Markovian dynamics and slowing down relaxation times.
method: The core method involves modifying the bath spectral density $J(\omega)$ by applying a sharp band-gap truncation followed by a smooth edge-softening convolution protocol.
model_or_system: The study analyzes open quantum systems, specifically using the Spin-Boson Model (SBM) and the Single-Impurity Anderson Model (SIAM), coupled to non-interacting bosonic or fermionic baths.
key_observables: Non-Markovianity measure ($N$), trace distance ($D(t)$), Concurrence (for two-spin setups), and spin polarization relaxation ($P(t)$).
important_parameters: The gap energy ($W_0$), the softening width ($\epsilon$), and the temperature ($T$) relative to $W_0$ are key tunable parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability to analytically continue the spectral density to the complex plane and assumes the spectral shaping protocol preserves the total hybridization strength.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spectral truncation and correlation functions for fermionic baths, and show the time evolution of the trace distance and non-Markovianity measure ($N$) as a function of the softening width $\epsilon$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the concept of non-Markovianity and the role of the bath correlation function $C(t)$. It then details the spectral shaping technique using band-gap truncation and edge-softening, demonstrating its applicability to both bosonic and fermionic baths, and finally presents numerical results showing the control over memory effects.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, physically implementable mechanism (spectral engineering) to control a fundamental resource (memory) in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant to quantum control and quantum information processing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Spectrum truncation and correlation functions for a fermionic bath. (a) Original bath spectral function (gray), truncated spectral function with a band gap of width 2W0 (black), softened gapped spectral functions (colored), and a scaled ungapped spectral function (gray dash-dot). All spec- tral functions have the same area below the curves except the original one. (b) Real part of the corresponding environment correlation functions.

Figure 2: Non-Markovianity control via environmental spec- trum engineering. Trace distance dynamics D(t) for (a) an SBM and (b) an SIAM at selected softening widths ϵ (color- coded). The parameter ϵ controls the band edge sharpness [cf. Eq. (5)]. The gray dash-dotted lines in (a) and (b) provide a benchmark for a scaled Lorentzian (ungapped) bath spec- tral function. (c) Non-Markovianity measure N versus ϵ for both models. The purple curve shows results from a virtual SIAM simulation with the fermionic parity replaced by the bosonic parity within the HEOM method. Model parameters are given in the main text.

Figure 3: Concurrence dynamics of two spins coupled to a common bath with tunable softening width ϵ. (a) Time evo- lution for selected ϵ (colored) and the benchmark for a scaled ungapped bath (gray dash-dotted). (b) Steady-state concur- rence Cst as a function of ϵ/ωs. Model parameters are given in the main text.

Figure 4: Relaxation dynamics of spin polarization in (a) an SBM and (b) an SIAM for selected softening widths ϵ. Gray dash-dotted lines are benchmarks for the scaled ungapped bath. (c) Relaxation time Tr versus ϵ for both models; the two curves exhibit a similar dependence on ϵ up to an overall scale factor. Model parameters are given in the main text.
